notes.front: What does a carburettor air temperature (CAT) indicator measure?
notes.back: The temperature of the induction air, measured at the carburettor entrance.
notes.explanation: Many treat it as an icing indicator, but the handbook says it also gives many other important items of information.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Carburetor Air Temperature (CAT) Indicator”, p. 10-21
notes.evidence: Measured at the carburetor entrance, carburetor air temperature (CAT) is regarded by many as an indication of induction system ice formation. Although it serves this purpose, it also provides many other important items of information.
notes.example: Like a thermometer hung in a building’s air intake, but reading the air about to enter the carburettor.

notes.front: What does a fuel pressure indicator show in some aircraft installations?
notes.back: The fuel pressure at each engine’s carburettor or fuel injection unit inlet.
notes.explanation: Each engine’s pressure is shown on its own gauge on the instrument panel.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Fuel Pressure Indicator”, p. 10-22
notes.evidence: In some aircraft installations, the fuel pressure is sensed at the carburetor or fuel injection unit inlet of each engine, and the pressure is indicated on individual gauges on the instrument panel.
notes.example: Like a garden-hose pressure gauge fitted at the tap, but reading the fuel arriving at the engine’s metering unit.

notes.front: What does the oil pressure indicator (oil pressure gauge) show?
notes.back: The pressure at which oil enters the engine from the pump.
notes.explanation: A loss of that pressure can warn of an exhausted oil supply, pump failure, burned-out bearings or ruptured oil lines, among other causes.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 6, “Oil Pressure Gauge”, p. 6-8
notes.evidence: oil pressure gauge indicates the pressure that oil enters the engine from the pump. This gauge warns of possible engine failure caused by an exhausted oil supply, failure of the oil pump, burned-out bearings, ruptured oil lines, or other causes that may be indicated by a loss of oil pressure.
notes.example: Like a blood-pressure reading for the engine: a sudden drop points to a problem somewhere in the circulation.

notes.front: What is a Bourdon tube?
notes.back: A coiled tube, fixed and open at one end and sealed and free at the other, that straightens under pressure.
notes.explanation: The higher the pressure, the more it straightens, so its movement follows the pressure.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Pressure Sensing Mechanisms”, p. 10-4
notes.evidence: The open end of this coiled tube is fixed in place and the other end is sealed and free to move. When pressure is directed into the open end of the tube, the unfixed portion of the coiled tube tends to straighten out. The higher the pressure, the more the tube straightens.
notes.example: Like a paper party blower that uncurls when you blow into it, but made of metal and recoiling precisely as pressure falls.

notes.front: Where is the bulb of an oil temperature indicator placed?
notes.back: Where it measures the oil’s temperature before the oil enters the engine’s hot sections.
notes.explanation: A flight-deck gauge wired to the bulb shows the temperature, and an oil cooling fault appears as an abnormal reading.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 6, “Oil Temperature Indicator”, p. 6-9
notes.evidence: the bulb is located so that it measures the temperature of the oil before it enters the engine’s hot sections. An oil temperature gauge in the flight deck is connected to the oil temperature bulb by electrical leads. The oil temperature is indicated on the gauge. Any malfunction of the oil cooling system appears as an abnormal reading.
notes.example: Like checking bathwater at the tap rather than in the tub, but for oil on its way into the engine.

notes.front: What does a fuel-flow meter measure?
notes.back: The amount of fuel delivered to the engine.
notes.explanation: In engine testing, flow can be measured by a direct, a pressure-based or a turbine sensor-based flow meter.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Fuel-Flow Meter”, p. 10-22
notes.evidence: The fuel-flow meter measures the amount of fuel delivered to the engine. During engine testing procedures, the fuel-flow to the engine can be measured by three different methods: a direct flow meter, a pressure-based flow meter, or a turbine sensor-based flow meter.
notes.example: Like the pump display at a filling station, but showing how fast fuel is going into the engine rather than into the tank.

notes.front: What is a fuel-flow transmitter in a turbine installation?
notes.back: An electrical unit with a turbine that spins faster as flow rises, increasing the signal to the indicator.
notes.explanation: It is mounted in the accessory section and measures flow between the engine-driven fuel pump and the fuel control.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Fuel-Flow Meter”, p. 10-22
notes.evidence: The fuel-flow transmitter is conveniently mounted in the engine’s accessory section and measures the fuel-flow between the engine-driven fuel pump and the fuel control device. The transmitter is an electrical device that contains a turbine that turns faster as the flow increases, which increases the electrical signal to the indicator.
notes.example: Like a small water wheel in a stream whose speed tells you how fast the water runs, but sending that speed as an electrical signal.

notes.front: What does a manifold pressure gauge indicate?
notes.back: Absolute pressure in the intake manifold, in inches of mercury ("Hg).
notes.explanation: Absolute pressure includes atmospheric pressure plus the pressure in the intake manifold.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Manifold Pressure Indicator”, p. 10-23
notes.evidence: Absolute pressure takes into account the atmospheric pressure plus the pressure in the intake manifold. To read the manifold pressure of the engines, a specially designed manifold pressure gauge that indicates absolute manifold pressure in inches of mercury ("Hg) is used.
notes.example: Like a barometer, but piped to the engine’s intake manifold instead of open to the room.

notes.front: What does the tachometer of a reciprocating engine show, and how is it graduated?
notes.back: Crankshaft rpm; it is calibrated in hundreds, with graduations every 100 rpm.
notes.explanation: The same system is used when testing the engine as in the aircraft installation.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Tachometer Indicator”, p. 10-23
notes.evidence: The tachometer for reciprocating engines shows the engine crankshaft rpm. The system used for testing the engine is the same as the system in the aircraft installation. The tachometer, often referred to as TACH, is calibrated in hundreds with graduations at every 100-rpm interval.
notes.example: Like a car’s rev counter, but reading an aircraft engine’s crankshaft speed.

notes.front: What is a mechanical tachometer?
notes.back: An indicator connected to the engine by a flexible drive shaft.
notes.explanation: They are found on small single-engine light aircraft, where the engine is a short distance from the instrument panel.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Mechanical Tachometers”, p. 10-28
notes.evidence: Mechanical tachometer indicating systems are found on small, single-engine light aircraft in which a short distance exists between the engine and the instrument panel. They consist of an indicator connected to the engine by a flexible drive shaft.
notes.example: Like an old car speedometer driven by a cable from the gearbox, but counting engine revolutions.

notes.front: How does a common electric tachometer system work?
notes.back: An engine-driven generator is wired to a synchronous motor in the indicator that mirrors its output.
notes.explanation: The generator’s frequency output is directly proportional to engine speed.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Electric Tachometers”, p. 10-30
notes.evidence: As the engine turns, so does the generator. The frequency output of the generator is directly proportional to the speed of the engine. It is connected via wires to a synchronous motor in the indicator that mirrors this output.
notes.example: Like a bicycle dynamo whose output rises with speed, but read by a motor in the flight-deck dial.

notes.front: What is a synchroscope?
notes.back: An instrument that shows whether two or more rotating devices, such as engines, are synchronised.
notes.explanation: It compares rpm, so it uses the output of the tachometer generators.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Synchroscope”, p. 10-31
notes.evidence: The synchroscope is an instrument that indicates whether two or more rotating devices, such as engines, are synchronized. Since synchroscopes compare rpm, they utilize the output from tachometer generators.
notes.example: Like watching two clocks’ second hands side by side, but for engine speeds.

notes.front: What is a thermocouple?
notes.back: A circuit of two unlike metals touching at two junctions; heating one junction more than the other produces a voltage.
notes.explanation: The General deck met the thermocouple as a source of electricity; here its voltage, directly proportional to temperature, is what cylinder head and exhaust gas temperature gauges read.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Thermocouple Temperature Indicators”, p. 10-37
notes.evidence: A thermocouple is a circuit or connection of two unlike metals. The metals are touching at two separate junctions. If one of the junctions is heated to a higher temperature than the other, an electromotive force is produced in the circuit. This voltage is directly proportional to the temperature.
notes.example: Like a battery with no chemicals, whose output comes only from one joint being hotter than the other.

notes.front: What does a cylinder head temperature (CHT) gauge read from?
notes.back: A thermocouple on the cylinder that tests show runs hottest in that installation.
notes.explanation: The thermocouple sits in a special gasket under a rear spark plug, or in a well in the top or rear of the cylinder head.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Cylinder Head Temperature Indicator”, p. 10-23
notes.evidence: Cylinder head temperatures are indicated by a gauge connected to a thermocouple attached to the cylinder, that tests show to be the hottest on an engine in a particular installation. The thermocouple may be placed in a special gasket located under a rear spark plug, or in a special well in the top or rear of the cylinder head.
notes.example: Like putting the only thermometer in the warmest room of a house, but on an engine cylinder.

notes.front: What principle does an electrical resistance thermometer work on?
notes.back: For most metals, electrical resistance changes as the metal’s temperature changes.
notes.explanation: The handbook states this as the principle on which a resistance thermometer operates.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Electrical Resistance Thermometer”, p. 10-36
notes.evidence: For most metals, electrical resistance changes as the temperature of the metal changes. This is the principle upon which a resistance thermometer operates.
notes.example: Like judging a kettle’s heat by how its element’s resistance changes, but with a sensing bulb in oil or air.

notes.front: What is the sensing element of a bimetallic thermometer?
notes.back: Two strips of dissimilar metals bonded together.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls this thermometer very useful in aviation.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Non-Electric Temperature Indicators”, p. 10-34
notes.evidence: A bimetallic thermometer is very useful in aviation. The temperature sensing element of a bimetallic thermometer is made of two dissimilar metals strips bonded together.
notes.example: Like a thermostat strip in an old electric iron, but coiled and moving a pointer.

notes.front: On a reciprocating engine, what is the exhaust gas temperature (EGT) indicator’s sensor?
notes.back: A thermocouple placed in the exhaust stream just after the cylinder port.
notes.explanation: It allows adjustment of the mixture, which has a large effect on engine temperature.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 6, “Exhaust Gas Temperature Indicating Systems”, p. 6-38
notes.evidence: The exhaust gas temperature indicator consists of a thermocouple placed in the exhaust stream just after the cylinder port. [Figure 6-60] It is then connected to the instrument in the instrument panel. This allows for the adjustment of the mixture, which has a large effect on engine temperature.
notes.example: Like a thermometer in a chimney flue, but just outside an engine cylinder’s exhaust port.

notes.front: What does a turbine inlet temperature (TIT) indicating system show?
notes.back: The temperature of the gases entering the turbine.
notes.explanation: Numerous thermocouples can be used, with their average voltage representing TIT.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Turbine Gas Temperature Indicating Systems”, p. 10-39
notes.evidence: A TIT indicating system provides a visual indication at the instrument panel of the temperature of gases entering the turbine. Numerous thermocouples can be used with the average voltage representing the TIT.
notes.example: Like an EGT gauge, but reporting the gas temperature at the turbine’s entrance rather than its exit.

notes.front: What does a torquemeter indicate?
notes.back: The amount of torque being produced at the propeller shaft.
notes.explanation: Most torque systems use oil pressure from a torque valve to show actual engine power output.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Torquemeter”, p. 10-24
notes.evidence: Most torque systems use an oil pressure output from a torque valve to indicate actual engine power output at various power settings. The torquemeter indicates the amount of torque being produced at the propeller shaft.
notes.example: Like a torque wrench’s dial, but reading the twisting force on a running propeller shaft.

notes.front: What is engine pressure ratio (EPR)?
notes.back: An indication of the thrust a turbofan is developing, from total pressures at the inlet (Pt2) and turbine exhaust (Pt7).
notes.explanation: Many aircraft types use it to set takeoff power.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Engine Pressure Ratio Indicator”, p. 10-54
notes.evidence: Engine pressure ratio (EPR) is an indication of the thrust being developed by a turbofan engine and is used to set power for takeoff on many types of aircraft. It is instrumented by total pressure pickups in the engine inlet (Pt2) and in the turbine exhaust (Pt7).
notes.example: Like judging a pump by comparing its outlet and inlet pressures, but for a whole jet engine.

notes.front: How are turbine engine tachometers calibrated?
notes.back: In percent rpm, with 100 percent corresponding to optimum turbine speed.
notes.explanation: This lets engines with very different actual rpm use similar operating procedures.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Tachometers”, p. 10-28
notes.evidence: Turbine engine tachometers are calibrated in percentage of rpm with 100 percent corresponding to optimum turbine speed. This allows similar operating procedures despite the varied actual engine rpm of different engines.
notes.example: Like a phone battery shown as a percentage rather than in milliamp-hours, but for engine speed.

notes.front: What do turbine engine oil pressure and temperature indicators guard against, and what does the pressure indicator usually show?
notes.back: Engine failure from inadequate lubrication and cooling; the pressure indicator usually shows oil pump discharge pressure.
notes.explanation: The handbook says the oil supply to critical areas must be monitored for this reason.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Engine Oil Pressure Indicator”, p. 10-55
notes.evidence: To guard against engine failure resulting from inadequate lubrication and cooling of the various engine parts, the oil supply to critical areas must be monitored. The oil pressure indicator usually shows the engine oil pump discharge pressure.
introduces: turbine engine oil pressure and temperature indicators
notes.example: Like the oil-pressure and temperature gauges on a lorry, but for a turbine engine’s oil supply.
uses: turbine engine oil pressure and temperature indicators

notes.front: On some aircraft, what does an engine warning light show?
notes.back: That fuel pressure or oil pressure is low.
notes.explanation: Such devices show only that a system is working or has failed to work, not a value.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Warning Systems”, p. 10-24
notes.evidence: Many of the miscellaneous gauges and devices indicate only that a system is functioning or has failed to function. On some aircraft, a warning light illuminates when the fuel pressure or oil pressure is low.
notes.example: Like a car’s red oil-can light, but for an aircraft engine’s fuel or oil pressure.

notes.front: What is a master caution light?
notes.back: A centrally wired light that draws the crew’s attention whenever a participating system or component needs attention.
notes.explanation: A separate annunciator describes the actual problem.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Warnings & Cautions Annunciator Panels”, p. 10-74
notes.evidence: Master caution lights are used to draw the attention of the crew to a critical situation in addition to an annunciator that describes the problem. These master caution lights are centrally wired and illuminate whenever any of the participating systems or components require attention.
notes.example: Like a phone’s notification badge: it says something needs you; the message itself says what.

notes.front: What is an electronic centralised aircraft monitor (ECAM)?
notes.back: A two-monitor system that helps transport aircraft crews monitor aircraft systems.
notes.explanation: It is designed to help with monitoring numerous gauges while also flying the aircraft.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Electronic Centralized Aircraft Monitor (ECAM)”, p. 10-68
notes.evidence: On transport category aircraft, this can mean monitoring numerous gauges in addition to maneuvering the aircraft. The electronic centralized aircraft monitoring (ECAM) system is designed to assist with this duty. An ECAM system has two CRT monitors. In newer aircraft, these may be LCD.
notes.example: Like a car’s central infotainment screen replacing a row of dials, but for a transport aircraft’s systems.

notes.front: What is an engine indicating and crew alerting system (EICAS)?
notes.back: A system that monitors aircraft systems for the pilot, displaying engine as well as airframe parameters.
notes.explanation: It performs many of the same functions as ECAM.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 4, “Engine Indicating & Crew Alerting System (EICAS)”, p. 4-16
notes.evidence: An engine indicating and crew alerting system (EICAS) performs many of the same functions as an ECAM system. The objective is still to monitor the aircraft systems for the pilot. All EICAS display engine, as well as airframe, parameters.
introduces: engine indicating and crew alerting system
notes.example: Like ECAM, but with its own layout and a standby computer behind two screens.
uses: engine indicating and crew alerting system

notes.front: What does the EICAS primary display (top monitor) show?
notes.back: Primary engine parameters, such as EPR and EGT, full time, plus advisories and warnings.
notes.explanation: Secondary engine parameters and non-engine system status go on the bottom screen.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Engine Indicating & Crew Alerting System (EICAS)”, p. 10-71
notes.evidence: EICAS provides full time primary engine parameters (EPR, N1, EGT) on the top, primary monitor. Advisories and warning are also shown there. Secondary engine parameters and nonengine system status are displayed on the bottom screen.
notes.example: Like the main dials of a car dashboard kept always visible, with less urgent readings on a second screen.

notes.front: What does a full authority digital engine control (FADEC) on a reciprocating engine do?
notes.back: It continuously monitors and controls ignition, timing and fuel mixture, delivery and injection as one integrated system.
notes.explanation: It reads conditions such as crankshaft speed and manifold pressure, then adjusts mixture and timing for each power setting.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 4, “FADEC System Description”, p. 4-14
notes.evidence: FADEC continuously monitors and controls ignition, timing, and fuel mixture/delivery/injection, and spark ignition as an integrated control system. FADEC monitors engine operating conditions (crankshaft speed, top dead center position, the induction manifold pressure, and the induction air temperature) and then automatically adjusts the fuel-to-air ratio mixture and ignition timing accordingly for any given power setting to attain optimum engine performance.
notes.example: Like a car’s engine management computer, but controlling an aircraft engine’s ignition and fuel injection.

notes.front: What is a slippage mark on an instrument?
notes.back: A white radial index line on the cover glass that shows any movement between the glass and the case.
notes.explanation: If the glass moved, the range and limit markings painted on it would be in the wrong place.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Engine Instruments”, p. 10-21
notes.evidence: When the markings appear on the cover glass, a white line is used as an index mark, often called a slippage mark. The white radial mark indicates any movement between the cover glass and the case, a condition that would cause mislocation of the other range and limit markings.
notes.example: Like a tamper stripe across a jar lid, but showing whether an instrument’s glass has turned.

notes.front: How is a fuel counter (totaliser) type fuel quantity indicator set?
notes.back: When the aircraft is refuelled, the counter is set by hand to the total pounds of fuel in all tanks.
notes.explanation: It is used to keep a record of fuel use.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel Quantity Indicating Units”, p. 2-46
notes.evidence: The fuel counter, or totalizer, is used to keep record of fuel use. When the aircraft is serviced with fuel, the counter is manually set to the total number of pounds of fuel in all tanks.
notes.example: Like a trip meter you reset at every fill-up, but counting pounds of fuel down instead of miles up.

notes.front: What conditions should a fuel pressure warning alert the pilot to?
notes.back: Low fuel pressure, as from a malfunctioning pump or a tank emptied too far to keep the pump’s output pressure.
notes.explanation: The handbook says such a condition requires the pilot’s immediate attention.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Fuel Pressure”, p. 10-9
notes.evidence: A malfunctioning fuel pump, or a tank that has been emptied beyond the point at which there is sufficient fuel entering the pump to maintain desired output pressure, is a condition that requires the pilot’s immediate attention.
notes.example: Like a low-water-pressure alarm on a boiler, but for the fuel reaching the engine.

notes.front: What are two instruments on the handbook’s list of basic engine instruments?
notes.back: Any two of its ten, such as the tachometer and the oil pressure gauge.
notes.explanation: The list also includes the CAT, fuel pressure, fuel-flow, manifold pressure, oil temperature, EGT and CHT gauges and the torquemeter.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Engine Instruments”, p. 10-21
notes.evidence: Some of the basic instruments are: 1. Carburetor air temperature gauge. 2. Fuel pressure gauge. 3. Fuel-flow meter. 4. Manifold pressure gauge. 5. Oil temperature gauge. 6. Oil pressure gauge. 7. Tachometer. 8. Exhaust gas temperature gauge. 9. Cylinder head temperature gauge. 10. Torquemeter.

notes.front: The term engine instruments usually includes {{c1::all instruments required to measure and indicate the functioning of the powerplant}}.
notes.back: All instruments required to measure and indicate the functioning of the powerplant.
notes.explanation: They are generally installed so that all of them can be seen at one time.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Engine Instruments”, p. 10-24
notes.evidence: The term engine instruments usually includes all instruments required to measure and indicate the functioning of the powerplant. The engine instruments are generally installed on the instrument panel so that all of them can easily be observed at one time.

notes.front: What does coordinating the flight-deck controls with the engine instrument readings protect against?
notes.back: Exceeding operating limits.
notes.explanation: Manifold pressure, rpm, engine temperature, oil temperature, CAT and mixture can all be controlled from the flight deck.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Engine Instruments”, p. 10-24
notes.evidence: Manifold pressure, rpm, engine temperature, oil temperature, CAT, and the air-fuel ratio can be controlled by manipulating the flight deck controls. Coordinating the movement of the controls with the instrument readings protects against exceeding operating limits.

notes.front: A student sorts gauges into “on the handbook’s basic engine instrument list” and “not on it”. Which belongs on the list?
notes.back: D) Cylinder head temperature gauge
notes.explanation: The handbook’s list of ten basic engine instruments includes the cylinder head temperature gauge.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Engine Instruments”, p. 10-21
notes.evidence: 7. Tachometer. 8. Exhaust gas temperature gauge. 9. Cylinder head temperature gauge. 10. Torquemeter.
notes.choices:
A) Hydraulic pressure gauge
B) Airspeed indicator
C) Altimeter
D) Cylinder head temperature gauge
notes.choicesExplained: A: an airframe system gauge; it is not on the engine list. B: a flight instrument, not one of the ten basic engine instruments. C: a flight instrument, not an engine instrument.

notes.front: On the handbook’s example CAT gauge, the yellow arc runs from {{c1::–10 °C to +15 °C}}, where the danger of icing occurs.
notes.explanation: The green arc, the normal range, follows from +15 °C to +40 °C.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Carburetor Air Temperature (CAT) Indicator”, p. 10-21
notes.evidence: The yellow arc indicates a range from –10 °C to +15 °C, since the danger of icing occurs between these temperatures. The green range indicates the normal operating range from +15 °C to +40 °C.

notes.front: On the handbook’s example CAT gauge, what does operating above the 40 °C red line risk?
notes.back: Detonation.
notes.explanation: The red line marks the maximum operating temperature of 40 °C.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Carburetor Air Temperature (CAT) Indicator”, p. 10-21
notes.evidence: The red line indicates the maximum operating temperature of 40 °C; any operation at a temperature over this value places the engine in danger of detonation.

notes.front: During a ground run the CAT gauge climbs steadily and keeps climbing. What does the handbook say this shows?
notes.back: D) A sustained induction system fire
notes.explanation: A backfire gives a momentary rise; a sustained induction fire shows as a continuous increase of CAT.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Carburetor Air Temperature (CAT) Indicator”, p. 10-21
notes.evidence: Backfiring is indicated as a momentary rise on the gauge, provided it is of sufficient severity for the heat to be sensed at the carburetor air-measuring point. A sustained induction system fire shows a continuous increase of CAT.
notes.choices:
A) A single backfire
B) Normal warm-up
C) Carburettor icing
D) A sustained induction system fire
notes.choicesExplained: A: a backfire shows only as a momentary rise. B: the handbook links a continuous CAT increase to an induction fire. C: icing is linked to the low yellow range, not a steady climb.

notes.front: On the handbook’s example carburettor-engine fuel pressure gauge, what do the red lines at 2 psi and 9 psi mark?
notes.back: The minimum fuel pressure allowed in flight (2 psi) and the maximum allowable fuel pressure (9 psi).
notes.explanation: The green arc between them, 2 to 9 psi, is the desired range.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Fuel Pressure Indicator”, p. 10-22
notes.evidence: The red line on the dial at the 2 pounds psi graduation shows the minimum fuel pressure allowed during flight. The green arc shows the desired range of operation, which is 2 to 9 psi. The red line at the 9 psi graduation indicates the maximum allowable fuel pressure.

notes.front: With fuel injection systems, the handbook gives a minimum allowable fuel pressure of approximately {{c1::10 psi}} and a maximum of generally 25 psi.
notes.back: Approximately 10 psi.
notes.explanation: Fuel injection systems run a much higher fuel pressure range than the carburettor example.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Fuel Pressure Indicator”, p. 10-22
notes.evidence: When fuel injection systems are used, the fuel pressure range is much higher; the minimum allowable pressure is approximately 10 psi, and the maximum is generally 25 psi.

notes.front: An owner wants a direct-reading fuel pressure gauge with a fuel line run into the flight deck. What does the Airframe handbook prefer?
notes.back: A) A transmitter that sends an electrical signal to the flight-deck indicator
notes.explanation: A fuel line in the flight deck is particularly undesirable because a leak could cause a fire, so the sensor sits in an electrical transmitter.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Fuel Pressure”, p. 10-10
notes.evidence: it is particularly undesirable to run a fuel line into the flight deck, due to the potential for fire should a leak develop. Therefore, the preferred arrangement is to have whichever sensing mechanism that is used be part of a transmitter device that uses electricity to send a signal to the indicator in the flight deck.
notes.choices:
A) A transmitter that sends an electrical signal to the flight-deck indicator
B) Removing the fuel pressure gauge altogether
C) Running the fuel line to the gauge, as proposed
D) A longer line so the gauge sits further from the pilot
notes.choicesExplained: B: the handbook says fuel pressure gauges give the pilot critical information. C: the handbook calls a fuel line into the flight deck particularly undesirable because of fire risk from a leak. D: the fuel would still be in the flight deck.

notes.front: What are two checks the handbook lists for a fuel pressure gauge?
notes.back: Any two, such as: pointer zero tolerance and oscillation, cover glass security and range markings, line leaks, vent obstruction.
notes.explanation: A defective instrument is to be replaced.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel Pressure Gauge”, p. 2-32
notes.evidence: Check the pointer for zero tolerance and excessive oscillation. Check the cover glass for looseness and for proper range markings. Check the lines and connections for leaks. Be sure that there is no obstruction in the vent. Replace the instrument if it is defective.

notes.front: You are checking a low fuel pressure warning light. The lamp works on its test switch. What does the handbook say to do next?
notes.back: C) Turn the battery switch on, build pressure with the booster pump and note the pressure at which the light goes out
notes.explanation: Building pressure with the booster pump and noting when the light goes out checks the switch point; the contacts are adjusted if necessary.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Pressure Warning Signal”, p. 2-33
notes.evidence: Check the lamp by pressing the test switch to see that it lights. Check the operation by turning the battery switch on, building up pressure with the booster pump, and observing the pressure at which the light goes out. If necessary, adjust the contact mechanism.
notes.choices:
A) Run the engine at full power and watch for the light
B) Replace the contact mechanism as routine
C) Turn the battery switch on, build pressure with the booster pump and note the pressure at which the light goes out
D) Disconnect the fuel line to confirm the light comes on
notes.choicesExplained: A: the check uses the booster pump, not an engine run. B: the mechanism is adjusted only if necessary. D: the handbook does not describe this.

notes.front: On the handbook’s example oil pressure gauge, what do 25 psi, 60–85 psi and 100 psi mark?
notes.back: Minimum in flight (red, 25), desired range (green, 60–85), maximum (red, 100).
notes.explanation: Actual markings for a given aircraft are in its specifications or Type Certificate Data Sheets.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Oil Pressure Indicator”, p. 10-22
notes.evidence: The actual markings for specific aircraft may be found in the aircraft specifications or Type Certificate Data Sheets. The lower red line at 25 psi indicates the minimum oil pressure permissible in flight. The green arc between 60 to 85 psi illustrates the desired operating oil pressure range. The red line at 100 psi indicates maximum permissible oil pressure.

notes.front: Just after start, the oil pressure gauge shows no pressure at all while the engine runs. What does the handbook say to do?
notes.back: C) Shut the engine down immediately
notes.explanation: If the gauge fails to register pressure with the engine running, the engine should be shut down immediately.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Oil Pressure Indicator”, p. 10-22
notes.evidence: The engine should be shut down immediately if the gauge fails to register pressure when the engine is operating.
notes.choices:
A) Increase rpm to raise pump output
B) Keep running for a few minutes to let the oil warm
C) Shut the engine down immediately
D) Tap the gauge and continue if the needle moves
notes.choicesExplained: A: running on with no indicated pressure is what the handbook rules out. B: the handbook says to shut down immediately. D: the rule for no pressure is an immediate shutdown.

notes.front: The oil pressure pointer swings back and forth excessively in steady running. Which cause does the handbook give?
notes.back: C) Air in the lines to the gauge, or an oil system unit working improperly
notes.explanation: Excessive pointer oscillation indicates air in the gauge lines or an oil system unit that is functioning improperly.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Oil Pressure Indicator”, p. 10-22
notes.evidence: Excessive oscillation of the gauge pointer indicates that there is air in the lines leading to the gauge, or that some unit of the oil system is functioning improperly.
notes.choices:
A) A normal reading for a cold engine
B) A slipped cover glass
C) Air in the lines to the gauge, or an oil system unit working improperly
D) Oil that is too cool to register
notes.choicesExplained: A: the handbook treats excessive oscillation as a fault sign. B: glass slippage misplaces the markings; it does not move the pointer. D: the handbook names air in the lines or a faulty unit.

notes.front: Why does a Bourdon-tube oil pressure gauge have a small restriction in its case or inlet?
notes.back: To stop the oil pump’s surging from damaging the gauge or making the pointer oscillate violently.
notes.explanation: Without it, each pump pulsation could damage the gauge or swing the pointer violently.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 6, “Oil Pressure Gauge”, p. 6-8
notes.evidence: This gauge is constructed similarly to other Bourdon-type gauges, except that it has a small restriction built into the instrument case, or into the nipple connection leading to the Bourdon tube. This restriction prevents the surging action of the oil pump from damaging the gauge or causing the pointer to oscillate too violently with each pressure pulsation.

notes.front: In cold weather, an oil pressure gauge whose line is filled with light oil reads sluggishly. What correction does the handbook give?
notes.back: A) Disconnect, drain and refill the gauge line with light oil
notes.explanation: Engine oil gradually mixes into the light oil; in cold weather the thicker mix makes readings sluggish, so the line is drained and refilled.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 6, “Oil Pressure Gauge”, p. 6-9
notes.evidence: In time, engine oil mixes with some of the light oil in the line to the transmitter; during cold weather, the thicker mixture causes sluggish instrument readings. To correct this condition, the gauge line must be disconnected, drained, and refilled with light oil.
notes.choices:
A) Disconnect, drain and refill the gauge line with light oil
B) Fill the line with engine oil instead
C) Replace the Bourdon tube
D) Adjust the oil pressure relief valve
notes.choicesExplained: B: engine oil mixing into the line is the cause. C: the fault is thick oil in the line, not the tube. D: that changes engine oil pressure, not the gauge line.

notes.front: A light aircraft’s oil temperature gauge has no electrical connection: a capillary tube runs from a bulb to the instrument. What mechanism is most likely inside?
notes.back: D) A Bourdon tube reading vapour pressure from a volatile liquid in the bulb
notes.explanation: Vapour pressure in the bulb rises and falls with temperature, and a Bourdon tube shows it on a dial marked in degrees.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Non-Electric Temperature Indicators”, p. 10-35
notes.evidence: By filling a sensing bulb with such a volatile liquid and connecting it to a bourdon tube, the tube causes an indication of the rising and falling vapor pressure due to temperature change. Calibration of the dial face in degrees Fahrenheit or Celsius, rather than psi, provides a temperature reading.
notes.choices:
A) A thermocouple
B) A ratiometer
C) A Wheatstone bridge
D) A Bourdon tube reading vapour pressure from a volatile liquid in the bulb
notes.choicesExplained: A: a thermocouple is electrical and needs leads to a voltmeter. B: a ratiometer is an electrical resistance indicator. C: a bridge circuit is electrical, not a capillary system.

notes.front: During test-cell run-in, where are oil temperatures taken and what do they show?
notes.back: At the oil inlet and outlet; they show whether heat transferred to the oil is low, normal or excessive.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls this of extreme importance when breaking in large reciprocating engines.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Oil Temperature Indicator”, p. 10-22
notes.evidence: During engine run-in in the test cell, engine oil temperature readings are taken at the oil inlet and outlet. From these readings, it can be determined if the engine heat transferred to the oil is low, normal, or excessive. This information is of extreme importance during the breaking-in process of large reciprocating engines.

notes.front: On the handbook’s example oil temperature gauge, what does the red mark at 245 °F indicate?
notes.back: The maximum permissible oil temperature.
notes.explanation: The green mark below 245 °F shows the desired temperature for continuous engine operation.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Oil Temperature Indicator”, p. 10-22
notes.evidence: The green mark between 25 °F and below 245 °F shows the desired oil temperature for continuous engine operation. The red mark at 245 °F indicates the maximum permissible oil temperature.

notes.front: You are fitting an oil temperature bulb on a wet-sump engine. Where does the handbook place it?
notes.back: D) Where it senses oil temperature after the oil passes through the oil cooler
notes.explanation: In a wet-sump engine the bulb senses oil after the cooler; in a dry-sump engine it may be anywhere in the inlet line.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 6, “Oil Temperature Indicator”, p. 6-9
notes.evidence: In dry-sump lubricating systems, the oil temperature bulb may be anywhere in the oil inlet line between the supply tank and the engine. Oil systems for wet-sump engines have the temperature bulb located where it senses oil temperature after the oil passes through the oil cooler.
notes.choices:
A) In the exhaust stream just after a cylinder port
B) Anywhere in the inlet line between supply tank and engine
C) In the hottest cylinder head
D) Where it senses oil temperature after the oil passes through the oil cooler
notes.choicesExplained: A: that is the EGT probe position. B: that is the dry-sump arrangement. C: that is where the CHT thermocouple goes.

notes.front: On a turbine engine, what does an oil inlet temperature indicator show besides oil temperature?
notes.back: Whether the engine oil cooler is operating properly.
notes.explanation: It shows the temperature of the oil as it enters the oil pressure pump.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Engine Oil Temperature Indicator”, p. 10-57
notes.evidence: An oil inlet temperature indicator frequently is provided to show the temperature of the oil as it enters the oil pressure pump. Oil inlet temperature is also an indication of proper operation of the engine oil cooler.
uses: turbine engine oil pressure and temperature indicators

notes.front: On light reciprocating aircraft, what often serves as the fuel-flow meter, and why does that work?
notes.back: The fuel pressure gauge; in that system fuel flow is proportional to fuel pressure.
notes.explanation: Such readings are normally in gallons per hour.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Fuel-Flow Meter”, p. 10-22
notes.evidence: Reciprocating engines on light aircraft usually use a fuel pressure gauge that is also used for the flow meter. This is because the fuel-flow is proportional to the fuel pressure in this system. Fuel-flow is normally measured in gallons per hour.

notes.front: A technician moving from piston twins to jets asks why the jet’s fuel-flow gauge reads in pounds per hour. What does the handbook say?
notes.back: C) Fuel weight is a major factor in the aerodynamics of large turbine aircraft
notes.explanation: Turbine fuel flow is shown in lb/hr instead of gallons because fuel weight matters so much to large turbine aircraft.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Fuel-Flow Indicator”, p. 10-55
notes.evidence: Fuel flow in turbine aircraft is measured in lb/hr instead of gallons, because the fuel weight is a major factor in the aerodynamics of large turbine aircraft. Fuel flow is of interest in monitoring fuel consumption and checking engine performance.
notes.choices:
A) Jet fuel cannot be measured by volume
B) It is required only for test cells
C) Fuel weight is a major factor in the aerodynamics of large turbine aircraft
D) Gallons are used only for avgas colour grades
notes.choicesExplained: A: the handbook gives weight’s importance, not a measuring limit. B: flight-deck turbine indicators also read in lb/hr. D: colour grades have nothing to do with flow units.

notes.front: After fuel is jettisoned, the crew notices the fuel counter still shows the jettisoned fuel as remaining. What does the handbook say?
notes.back: A) This is expected: jettisoned fuel still shows as available on the counter
notes.explanation: The counter subtracts only fuel measured by the flow meter, so jettisoned fuel and upstream leaks are not counted.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel Quantity Indicating Units”, p. 2-46
notes.evidence: However, there are certain conditions that cause the fuel counter indication to be inaccurate. Any jettisoned fuel is indicated on the fuel counter as fuel still available for use. Any fuel that leaks from a tank or a fuel line upstream of the flow meter is not counted.
notes.choices:
A) This is expected: jettisoned fuel still shows as available on the counter
B) The counter subtracts jettisoned fuel automatically
C) The flow meter has failed
D) Only leaks cause this error
notes.choicesExplained: B: the handbook says it does not. C: the counter only subtracts fuel passing through the flow meter to the engine. D: leaks upstream of the flow meter are another uncounted loss, not the only one.

notes.front: On a manifold pressure gauge, what does the red line indicate?
notes.back: The maximum manifold pressure permissible during takeoff.
notes.explanation: Range markings vary with different kinds of engines and installations.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Manifold Pressure Indicator”, p. 10-23
notes.evidence: The red line indicates the maximum manifold pressure permissible during takeoff.

notes.front: Before starting a normally aspirated engine at a sea-level airfield, what should the manifold pressure gauge read?
notes.back: C) About atmospheric pressure, approximately 30 "Hg
notes.explanation: With the engine not running, the gauge should read approximate atmospheric pressure, about 30 "Hg at sea level and less at higher fields.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Engine Starting”, p. 10-25
notes.evidence: Before starting the engine, observe the manifold pressure gauge that should read approximate atmospheric (barometric) pressure when the engine is not running. At sea level, this is approximately 30 "Hg, and at fields above sea level, the atmospheric pressure is less, depending on the height above sea level.
notes.choices:
A) Zero, because the engine is stopped
B) The takeoff red-line value
C) About atmospheric pressure, approximately 30 "Hg
D) About 15 "Hg
notes.choicesExplained: A: it reads absolute pressure, so it shows atmospheric pressure at rest. B: that is the maximum permissible during takeoff. D: at sea level the handbook gives approximately 30 "Hg.

notes.front: Two aircraft at full power: one normally aspirated, one turbocharged. Which statement about their manifold pressure matches the Airframe handbook?
notes.back: C) Only the turbocharged engine can read above ambient atmospheric pressure
notes.explanation: Normally aspirated engines peak slightly below ambient; turbocharged or supercharged engines show full power above ambient.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Manifold Pressure”, p. 10-8
notes.evidence: For normally aspirated engines, maximum manifold pressure would be slightly less than the ambient atmospheric pressure. Turbocharged or supercharged engines pressurize the air being mixed with the fuel, so full power indications are above the ambient atmospheric pressure.
notes.choices:
A) Both read exactly ambient
B) Both read above ambient at full power
C) Only the turbocharged engine can read above ambient atmospheric pressure
D) The normally aspirated engine reads higher
notes.choicesExplained: A: the turbocharged engine pressurises its intake air. B: a normally aspirated engine peaks slightly below ambient. D: it cannot exceed ambient; the turbocharged one can.

notes.front: During takeoff the tachometer needle passes the red line. What does the handbook call this condition?
notes.back: B) An overspeed condition
notes.explanation: The red line marks the maximum rpm permissible during takeoff; any rpm beyond it is an overspeed.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Tachometer Indicator”, p. 10-23
notes.evidence: The red line indicates the maximum rpm permissible during takeoff; any rpm beyond this value is an overspeed condition.
notes.choices:
A) Normal takeoff operation
B) An overspeed condition
C) A caution range only
D) Slippage of the cover glass
notes.choicesExplained: A: the red line is the maximum rpm permissible during takeoff. C: caution is yellow; beyond the red line is overspeed. D: slippage concerns the markings, not the rpm.

notes.front: A twin has its engines on the wings, far from the instrument panel. Which tachometer type does the handbook point to?
notes.back: C) Electric tachometers
notes.explanation: Where the engine is not just forward of the panel, mechanical linkage is impractical, and electric tachometers give greater accuracy with lower maintenance.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Electric Tachometers”, p. 10-29
notes.evidence: It is not practical to use a mechanical linkage between the engine and the rpm indicator on aircraft with engines not mounted in the fuselage just forward of the instrument panel. Greater accuracy with lower maintenance is achieved through the use of electric tachometers.
notes.choices:
A) Flexible-shaft mechanical tachometers
B) Manifold pressure gauges
C) Electric tachometers
D) Synchroscopes alone
notes.choicesExplained: A: a mechanical linkage is not practical when engines are not just forward of the panel. B: these measure pressure, not rpm. D: a synchroscope compares speeds; it does not show rpm.

notes.front: What maintenance does a magnetic pickup rpm system need?
notes.back: Little beyond setting the clearance between the gear teeth and the pickup.
notes.explanation: The pickup counts gear-tooth edges as electrical pulses to give shaft rpm.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Tachometer Check”, p. 10-64
notes.evidence: By counting the amount of pulses, the rpm of the shaft is obtained. This type of system requires little maintenance, other than setting the clearance between the gear teeth and the magnetic pickup.

notes.front: When checking a tachometer indicator, what is the usual limit for the change in reading after lightly tapping it?
notes.back: Approximately 15 rpm, though the indicator manufacturer’s tolerance may differ.
notes.explanation: Indicators are also checked for loose glass, chipped scale markings and loose pointers.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Tachometer Maintenance”, p. 10-81
notes.evidence: Tachometer indicators should be checked for loose glass, chipped scale markings, or loose pointers. The difference in indications between readings taken before and after lightly tapping the instrument should not exceed approximately 15 rpm. This value may vary, depending on the tolerance established by the indicator manufacturer.

notes.front: At idle, an electric tachometer’s pointer fluctuates and reads low, then steadies as rpm rises. What does the handbook say this indicates?
notes.back: C) The synchronous motor is not yet synchronised with the generator output
notes.explanation: At idle the motor may not be synchronised; it should synchronise and read correctly as speed increases.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Tachometer Maintenance”, p. 10-81
notes.evidence: When an engine equipped with an electrical tachometer is running at idle rpm, the tachometer indicator pointers may fluctuate and read low. This is an indication that the synchronous motor is not synchronized with the generator output. As the engine speed is increased, the motor should synchronize and register the rpm correctly.
notes.choices:
A) The tach generator must be replaced
B) A broken flexible drive shaft
C) The synchronous motor is not yet synchronised with the generator output
D) A slipped cover glass
notes.choicesExplained: A: the handbook expects synchronisation as speed rises. B: electric tachometers have no drive shaft to the indicator. D: that misplaces markings; it does not make the pointer fluctuate.

notes.front: A trainee asks what a turbine engine tachometer is mainly for. Which answer matches the handbook?
notes.back: C) Monitoring rpm in normal running and during start, and showing any overspeed
notes.explanation: The main purpose of the tachometer is to monitor rpm normally and during start, and to indicate an overspeed.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Tachometer”, p. 10-55
notes.evidence: The main purpose of the tachometer is to be able to monitor rpm under normal conditions, during an engine start, and to indicate an overspeed condition, if one occurs.
notes.choices:
A) Measuring propeller shaft torque
B) Setting takeoff thrust on turbofans
C) Monitoring rpm in normal running and during start, and showing any overspeed
D) Showing turbine gas temperature
notes.choicesExplained: A: that is the torquemeter’s job. B: EPR is used to set takeoff power on many types. D: EGT or TIT indicators do that.

notes.front: A CHT thermocouple is fitted to one cylinder only. Detonation starts in a different cylinder. What does the handbook say about the CHT reading?
notes.back: B) It will not show the detonation, which is indicated only if it occurs in the thermocouple’s cylinder
notes.explanation: One thermocouple gives only general engine temperature; detonation is not indicated unless it occurs in that cylinder.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Cylinder Head Temperature Indicator”, p. 10-24
notes.evidence: Since the thermocouple is attached to only one cylinder, it can do no more than give evidence of general engine temperature. While normally it can be assumed that the remaining cylinder temperatures are lower, conditions such as detonation are not indicated unless they occur in the cylinder that has the thermocouple attached.
notes.choices:
A) It will rise sharply
B) It will not show the detonation, which is indicated only if it occurs in the thermocouple’s cylinder
C) It will read the average of all cylinders
D) It will read outside air temperature
notes.choicesExplained: A: the handbook says detonation elsewhere is not indicated. C: one thermocouple gives only general engine temperature. D: that happens only with a cold, stopped engine.

notes.front: An engine has stood overnight at ambient temperature. Before starting it, the CHT gauge reads the same as the outside air temperature. What does this suggest?
notes.back: D) The instrument is working correctly
notes.explanation: At ambient temperature the CHT indicator should show free outside air temperature; the handbook calls this one test that it works.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 6, “Cylinder Temperature Indicating Systems”, p. 6-37
notes.evidence: Prior to operating the engine, provided it is at ambient temperature, the cylinder head temperature indicator indicates the free outside air temperature; that is one test for determining that the instrument is working correctly.
notes.choices:
A) The thermocouple lead is open
B) The gauge glass has slipped
C) The engine has a hydraulic lock
D) The instrument is working correctly
notes.choicesExplained: A: reading outside air temperature at ambient is the expected result. B: slippage misplaces markings; it does not set the reading. C: a CHT reading says nothing about hydraulic lock.

notes.front: With the engine running, the CHT pointer fluctuates. What should be checked first?
notes.back: All of the electrical connections.
notes.explanation: The bayonet or gasket should also be inspected for cleanness and security.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 6, “Cylinder Temperature Indicating Systems”, p. 6-38
notes.evidence: The bayonet or gasket should be inspected for cleanness and security of mounting. When operating the engine, all of the electrical connections should be checked if the cylinder head temperature pointer fluctuates.

notes.front: While replacing a CHT thermocouple, you find the lead is too long for the run. What does the handbook say to do?
notes.back: B) Coil and tie up the excess; do not cut it
notes.explanation: The thermocouple is designed to produce a given resistance, so reducing lead length gives an incorrect temperature reading.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 6, “Cylinder Temperature Indicating Systems”, p. 6-37
notes.evidence: When installing a thermocouple lead, remember not to cut off the lead because it is too long, but coil and tie up the excess length. The thermocouple is designed to produce a given amount of resistance. If the length of the lead is reduced, an incorrect temperature reading results.
notes.choices:
A) Cut it to length and re-terminate it
B) Coil and tie up the excess; do not cut it
C) Replace it with a shorter lead of any metal
D) Splice in a copper wire to reroute it
notes.choicesExplained: A: shortening the lead changes its resistance and gives a wrong reading. C: the lead’s resistance and metals are fixed by design. D: leads must match the metals of the thermocouple.

notes.front: Which metal pairs are common for CHT thermocouples, and which for turbine EGT?
notes.back: CHT: iron and constantan, or copper and constantan. Turbine EGT: chromel and alumel.
notes.explanation: Lead metals depend on the maximum temperature they are exposed to.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Thermocouple Temperature Indicators”, p. 10-37
notes.evidence: Thermocouple leads are made from a variety of metals, depending on the maximum temperature to which they are exposed. Iron and constantan, or copper and constantan, are common for CHT measurement. Chromel and alumel are used for turbine EGT thermocouples.

notes.front: With the thermocouple leads disconnected from a CHT indicator, what should the indicator read?
notes.back: B) The temperature of the flight deck around the instrument panel
notes.explanation: The handbook says the temperature around the instrument panel can then be read on the dial.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Thermocouple Temperature Indicators”, p. 10-38
notes.evidence: When the leads are disconnected from the indicator, the temperature of the flight deck area around the instrument panel can be read on the indicator dial.
notes.choices:
A) Zero
B) The temperature of the flight deck around the instrument panel
C) Full-scale
D) The last engine temperature
notes.choicesExplained: A: the compensated cold junction makes it show local temperature. C: an open circuit does not drive the pointer to full scale here. D: the indicator has no memory of earlier readings.

notes.front: Electrical resistance thermometers measure low and medium temperatures in the {{c1::–70 °C to 150 °C}} range.
notes.explanation: They are used for carburettor air, oil and free air temperatures, among others.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Electrical Resistance Thermometer”, p. 10-36
notes.evidence: Electrical resistance thermometers are used widely in many types of aircraft to measure carburetor air, oil, free air temperatures, and more. They are used to measure low and medium temperatures in the –70 °C to 150 °C range.

notes.front: An aircraft’s supply voltage varies widely and an accurate oil temperature reading is needed. Which indicator does the handbook favour?
notes.back: B) A ratiometer electrical resistance thermometer
notes.explanation: The Wheatstone bridge is subject to line-voltage errors; the ratiometer is more stable and can be more accurate.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Ratiometer Electrical Resistance Thermometers”, p. 10-37
notes.evidence: The Wheatstone-bridge indicator is subject to errors from line voltage fluctuation. The ratiometer is more stable and can deliver higher accuracy.
notes.choices:
A) A Wheatstone-bridge indicator
B) A ratiometer electrical resistance thermometer
C) A mercury thermometer
D) A synchroscope
notes.choicesExplained: A: it is subject to errors from line voltage fluctuation. C: the handbook says it has no application in aviation. D: it compares engine speeds, not temperatures.

notes.front: Thermocouple or electrical resistance thermometer: which measures high temperatures such as CHT and turbine EGT?
notes.back: The thermocouple, used to measure high temperatures.
notes.explanation: The handbook names CHT and turbine EGT as two common thermocouple applications.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Thermocouple Temperature Indicators”, p. 10-37
notes.evidence: Thermocouples are used to measure high temperatures. Two common applications are the measurement of cylinder head temperature (CHT) in reciprocating engines and exhaust gas temperature (EGT) in turbine engines.

notes.front: The handbook lists EGT, TIT and three other turbine gas temperatures. Which temperature are they all relative to?
notes.back: The temperature of the gases entering the first-stage turbine inlet guide vanes.
notes.explanation: Each engine takes its reading at one location, but all relate to that temperature.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Exhaust Gas Temperature Indicator (EGT)”, p. 10-55
notes.evidence: Exhaust gas temperature (EGT), turbine inlet temperature, (TIT), turbine gas temperature (TGT), interstage turbine temperature (ITT), and turbine outlet temperature (TOT) are all relative temperatures used to monitor the temperature of the exhaust gases entering the first stage turbine inlet guide vanes.

notes.front: A student asks why most large turbine engines sense temperature at the turbine discharge rather than the turbine inlet. What does the handbook say?
notes.back: A) Measuring turbine inlet temperature is impractical in most engines, and discharge temperature gives a relative indication
notes.explanation: Inlet gas temperature is the most critical variable but impractical to measure in most engines, so discharge thermocouples give a relative indication.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Exhaust Gas Temperature Indicator (EGT)”, p. 10-55
notes.evidence: However, it is impractical to measure turbine inlet temperature in most engines, especially large engines. Consequently, temperature thermocouples are inserted at the turbine discharge, where the temperature provides a relative indication of that at the inlet.
notes.choices:
A) Measuring turbine inlet temperature is impractical in most engines, and discharge temperature gives a relative indication
B) The inlet temperature is not an engine limit
C) Discharge temperature is higher and easier to read
D) Regulations forbid probes near the inlet
notes.choicesExplained: B: the inlet temperature is the most critical variable. C: it is much lower than inlet temperature. D: the handbook gives impracticality, not a ban.

notes.front: What does the flight-deck EGT indicator on a turbine engine show?
notes.back: The average of the temperatures measured by several thermocouples spaced around the exhaust duct.
notes.explanation: The thermocouples sit near the turbine exit.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Exhaust Gas Temperature Indicator (EGT)”, p. 10-55
notes.evidence: Several thermocouples are usually used, that are spaced at intervals around the perimeter of the engine exhaust duct near the turbine exit. The EGT indicator in the flight deck shows the average temperature measured by the individual thermocouples.

notes.front: Which instrument does the handbook say turboprops are usually fitted with to indicate power, instead of EPR?
notes.back: B) A torquemeter
notes.explanation: Only 10 to 15 percent of a turboprop’s thrust comes from jet thrust, so EPR is not used; a torquemeter measures shaft torque instead.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Torquemeter (Turboprop Engines)”, p. 10-55
notes.evidence: Only 10 to 15 percent of the thrust produced by a turboprop engine is from propulsive force derived from the jet thrust exiting the exhaust. Engine pressure ratio is not used as an indicator of the power produced by a turboprop engine. Turboprops are usually fitted with a torquemeter
notes.choices:
A) An EPR gauge
B) A torquemeter
C) A synchroscope
D) A manifold pressure gauge
notes.choicesExplained: A: EPR is not used as a turboprop power indicator. C: it compares engine speeds; it does not indicate power. D: that is a reciprocating-engine instrument.

notes.front: In an oil-pressure torquemeter, what makes the oil pressure proportional to propeller-shaft torque?
notes.back: A helical ring gear moves against a piston that controls a valve metering the oil pressure.
notes.explanation: A transducer usually turns the oil pressure into an electrical signal for the flight deck.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Torquemeter (Turboprop Engines)”, p. 10-55
notes.evidence: This gear moves against a piston that controls the opening of a valve, which controls the oil pressure flow. This action makes the oil pressure proportional to torque being applied at the propeller shaft. Generally, transducer is used to transfer the oil pressure into an electrical signal to be read by the flight deck instrument.

notes.front: Why must a turboprop torquemeter be calibrated at intervals?
notes.back: It is used to set power, so its accuracy must be assured.
notes.explanation: Readouts are normally in lb/ft of torque or percent horsepower.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Torquemeter (Turboprop Engines)”, p. 10-55
notes.evidence: The read out in the flight deck is normally in lb/ft of torque, or percent horsepower. The torquemeter is very important as it is used to set power settings. This instrument must be calibrated at intervals to assure its accuracy.

notes.front: What two pressures does the EPR gauge compare?
notes.back: Total exhaust pressure and the pressure of the ram air at the engine inlet.
notes.explanation: Because it compares two pressures, it is a differential pressure gauge.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Engine Pressure Ratio (EPR)”, p. 10-9
notes.evidence: This gauge compares the total exhaust pressure to the pressure of the ram air at the inlet of the engine. With adjustments for temperature, altitude, and other factors, the EPR gauge presents an indication of the thrust being developed by the engine. Since the EPR gauge compares two pressures, it is a differential pressure gauge.

notes.front: A technician must classify the EPR gauge by how it senses. Which description fits the Airframe handbook?
notes.back: D) A remote-sensing differential pressure gauge fed by a pressure ratio transmitter or a computer
notes.explanation: The EPR gauge compares two pressures and receives its input from an engine pressure ratio transmitter or, in digital displays, a computer.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Engine Pressure Ratio (EPR)”, p. 10-9
notes.evidence: Since the EPR gauge compares two pressures, it is a differential pressure gauge. It is a remote-sensing instrument that receives its input from an engine pressure ratio transmitter or, in digital instrument systems displays, from a computer.
notes.choices:
A) An absolute pressure gauge like manifold pressure
B) A direct-reading Bourdon tube gauge
C) A thermocouple indicator
D) A remote-sensing differential pressure gauge fed by a pressure ratio transmitter or a computer
notes.choicesExplained: A: EPR compares two pressures, so it is differential. B: EPR is remote-sensing, from a transmitter or computer. C: EPR compares pressures, not temperatures.

notes.front: On annunciator panels, what do green, yellow and red lights mean?
notes.back: Green: satisfactory. Yellow: caution, needs monitoring. Red: unsatisfactory, needs immediate attention or action.
notes.explanation: Standardised colours let the pilot tell messages apart.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Warnings & Cautions Annunciator Panels”, p. 10-73
notes.evidence: Standardized colors are used to differentiate between visual messages. For example, the color green indicates a satisfactory condition. Yellow is used to caution of a serious condition that requires further monitoring. Red is the color for an unsatisfactory condition which needs immediate attention or action.

notes.front: A master caution light comes on with a low oil pressure annunciator. The pilot cancels the master caution. What happens?
notes.back: C) The oil pressure annunciator stays lit until the fault is fixed; the master caution is reset for any new fault
notes.explanation: Cancelling resets the master caution to warn of later faults, while the specific annunciator stays lit until the cause is corrected.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Warnings & Cautions Annunciator Panels”, p. 10-74
notes.evidence: Once notified, the pilot may cancel the master caution, but a dedicated system or component annunciator light stays illuminated until the situation that caused the warning is rectified. Cancelling resets the master caution lights to warn of a subsequent fault event even before the initial fault is corrected.
notes.choices:
A) Both lights go out and the fault is cleared
B) The master caution cannot be cancelled until the fault is fixed
C) The oil pressure annunciator stays lit until the fault is fixed; the master caution is reset for any new fault
D) Cancelling disables warnings for that flight
notes.choicesExplained: A: the dedicated annunciator stays on until the situation is rectified. B: the pilot may cancel it once notified. D: cancelling resets it to warn of a later fault.

notes.front: Which of these flight-deck items tells the pilot only that a system has or has not failed, rather than giving a value?
notes.back: C) A low oil pressure warning light
notes.explanation: The handbook says warning devices indicate only that a system is functioning or has failed to function.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Warning Systems”, p. 10-24
notes.evidence: Many of the miscellaneous gauges and devices indicate only that a system is functioning or has failed to function. On some aircraft, a warning light illuminates when the fuel pressure or oil pressure is low.
notes.choices:
A) An oil pressure gauge
B) A fuel-flow meter
C) A low oil pressure warning light
D) A tachometer
notes.choicesExplained: A: it shows a value in psi. B: it shows an amount of flow. D: it shows rpm.

notes.front: How are EICAS’s two computers used?
notes.back: Both monitors receive information from the same computer; the second computer is a standby.
notes.explanation: Only one computer feeds both screens; the other waits as a standby.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Engine Indicating & Crew Alerting System (EICAS)”, p. 10-71
notes.evidence: EICAS is also a two-monitor, two-computer system with a display select panel. Both monitors receive information from the same computer. The second computer serves as a standby.

notes.front: What traditional gauge does an EICAS aircraft keep?
notes.back: A standby combination engine gauge, for total system failure.
notes.explanation: Otherwise traditional gauges are not used.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 4, “Engine Indicating & Crew Alerting System (EICAS)”, p. 4-16
notes.evidence: Traditional gauges are not utilized, other than a standby combination engine gauge in case of total system failure.

notes.front: A pilot suspects an engine problem developing in flight and wants maintenance to see the data later. What EICAS feature helps?
notes.back: C) Pressing the event record button on the display select panel
notes.explanation: The event record button records that flight period’s parameters for maintenance to study later.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Engine Indicating & Crew Alerting System (EICAS)”, p. 10-71
notes.evidence: Pilots that suspect a problem may be occurring during flight can press the event record button on the display select panel. This also records the parameters for that flight period to be studied later by maintenance.
notes.choices:
A) Pressing press to test on the annunciator panel
B) Cancelling the master caution
C) Pressing the event record button on the display select panel
D) Switching to the standby engine gauge
notes.choicesExplained: A: that only tests lights and circuits. B: that resets the caution light; it records nothing. D: the standby gauge is for total system failure.

notes.front: What are two of the four basic ECAM modes?
notes.back: Any two of: flight phase, advisory, failure related, manual.
notes.explanation: Of the four, the flight phase mode is normally used.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Electronic Centralized Aircraft Monitor (ECAM)”, p. 10-69
notes.evidence: There are four basic modes to the ECAM system: flight phase, advisory, failure related, and manual. The flight phase mode is normally used.

notes.front: A pilot has an ECAM system diagram selected in manual mode when a failure occurs. What happens to the display?
notes.back: A) The failure-related mode takes precedence over the selected mode
notes.explanation: The failure-related mode takes precedence over all other modes, whichever mode is selected at the time.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Electronic Centralized Aircraft Monitor (ECAM)”, p. 10-69
notes.evidence: The same is true for the failure-related mode, which takes precedent over all other modes regardless of which mode is selected at the time of the failure.
notes.choices:
A) The failure-related mode takes precedence over the selected mode
B) The manual view stays until the pilot clears it
C) ECAM switches to flight phase mode
D) Both monitors go blank
notes.choicesExplained: B: a failure warning cancels the manual view. C: failure-related mode overrides all others. D: ECAM shows the failure and a system schematic.

notes.front: Early ECAM or EICAS: which left engine parameters on traditional full-time flight-deck gauges?
notes.back: Early ECAM, which monitored only airframe systems.
notes.explanation: Later model ECAM systems added engine displays as well as airframe ones.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Electronic Centralized Aircraft Monitor (ECAM)”, p. 10-68
notes.evidence: Early ECAM systems only monitor airframe systems. Engine parameters are displayed on traditional full-time flight deck gauges. Later model ECAM systems incorporate engine displays, as well as airframe.

notes.front: How does a PowerLink FADEC tell the pilot about its own condition?
notes.back: It runs self-diagnostics and shows the result on the health status annunciator panel.
notes.explanation: The self-diagnostics determine the overall system status.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 4, “FADEC System Description”, p. 4-14
notes.evidence: As a control device, the system performs self-diagnostics to determine overall system status and conveys this information to the pilot by various indicators on the health status annunciator (HSA) panel.

notes.front: In a PowerLink FADEC, why is exhaust gas temperature measured after each burn?
notes.back: B) To verify that the fuel-to-air ratio calculations were correct for that combustion event
notes.explanation: Measuring EGT after the burn checks the computer’s fuel-to-air calculation for that combustion event.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 4, “FADEC System Description”, p. 4-15
notes.evidence: Exhaust gas temperature is measured after the burn to verify that the fuel-to-air ratio calculations were correct for that combustion event.
notes.choices:
A) To set the ignition timing for start
B) To verify that the fuel-to-air ratio calculations were correct for that combustion event
C) To replace the tachometer signal
D) Only to drive a flight-deck gauge
