notes.choicesExplained: A: timing comes from speed and manifold pressure. C: engine speed comes from the speed sensor assembly. D: the handbook says it checks the fuel-to-air calculation.

notes.front: What does a red line (radial) on an engine instrument indicate?
notes.back: A point beyond which a dangerous operating condition exists.
notes.explanation: It marks a single limit point rather than a range.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Engine Instruments”, p. 10-21
notes.evidence: A red line, or mark, indicates a point beyond which a dangerous operating condition exists.

notes.front: A reciprocating-engine tachometer has a red arc in its middle. What does the handbook say about operating there?
notes.back: D) The arc can be passed through, but the engine cannot be operated in it
notes.explanation: A red arc marks a dangerous range, generally an engine–propeller vibration range: pass through it, do not operate in it.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Engine Instruments”, p. 10-21
notes.evidence: A red arc indicates a dangerous operating range due generally to an engine propeller vibration range. This arc can be passed through, but the engine cannot be operated in this area.
notes.choices:
A) It is the normal cruise range
B) It may be used for up to 5 minutes
C) It marks maximum rpm
D) The arc can be passed through, but the engine cannot be operated in it
notes.choicesExplained: A: normal range is green. B: the handbook gives no time allowance for a red arc. C: maximum is a red radial line.

notes.front: On an engine instrument, what do the yellow arc and the green arc show?
notes.back: Yellow: a range of caution. Green: a normal and safe range of operation.
notes.explanation: The yellow arc is generally on the outer edge of the cover glass or dial face.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Engine Instruments”, p. 10-21
notes.evidence: The yellow arc covers a given range of operation and is an indication of caution. Generally, the yellow arc is located on the outer circumference of the instrument cover glass or dial face. The green arc shows a normal and safe range of operation.

notes.front: Where are blue and white range markings used?
notes.back: On airspeed indicators, to define specific conditions.
notes.explanation: Green and yellow keep their usual meanings of normal range and caution.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Instrument Range Markings”, p. 10-80
notes.evidence: Green indicates the normal operating range. Yellow is used to indicate caution. Blue and white are used on airspeed indicators to define specific conditions.

notes.front: An approved replacement oil pressure gauge arrives without range markings. What does the Airframe handbook say?
notes.back: B) The technician may apply them, but only in accordance with approved data
notes.explanation: Correct marking is crucial, so a technician marking an approved replacement must use approved data only.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Instrument Range Markings”, p. 10-79
notes.evidence: Occasionally, the aircraft technician may find it necessary to apply these marking to an approved replacement instrument on which they do not appear. It is crucial that the instrument be marked correctly and only in accordance with approved data.
notes.choices:
A) Copy the markings from a similar aircraft
B) The technician may apply them, but only in accordance with approved data
C) Only the instrument maker may ever apply markings
D) Leave it unmarked; markings are optional
notes.choicesExplained: A: markings must follow approved data for this aircraft. C: the technician may sometimes need to apply them. D: the handbook says correct marking is crucial.

notes.front: On preflight, the white slippage mark on an engine gauge is broken: the glass half no longer lines up with the case half. What does this mean?
notes.back: D) The glass has rotated, so the range markings on it may be misplaced
notes.explanation: If the glass rotates in the bezel, markings on it no longer align with the dial; the broken mark shows this.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Instrument Range Markings”, p. 10-79
notes.evidence: A white slippage mark is made to extend from the glass to the instrument case. Should the glass rotate in the bezel, the marking will no longer be aligned properly with the calibrated instrument dial. The broken slippage mark indicates this to the pilot or technician.
notes.choices:
A) The pointer has come loose
B) The instrument is reading correctly
C) The gauge’s internal calibration has drifted
D) The glass has rotated, so the range markings on it may be misplaced
notes.choicesExplained: A: the slippage mark concerns the glass and case. B: a broken slippage mark means the markings may no longer align. C: the mark shows glass movement, not calibration.

notes.front: An EGT indicator has an internal fault. What may an A&P technician do?
notes.back: B) Remove it and have it repaired at a facility equipped for the work, usually a repair station
notes.explanation: Internal maintenance must be done at facilities with the specialised equipment it needs.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Maintenance of Instruments & Instrument Systems”, p. 10-80
notes.evidence: An FAA airframe and powerplant (A&P) technician is not qualified to do internal maintenance on instruments and related line replaceable units discussed in this chapter. This must be carried out at facilities equipped with the specialized equipment needed to perform the maintenance properly.
notes.choices:
A) Open the case and repair the movement
B) Remove it and have it repaired at a facility equipped for the work, usually a repair station
C) Recalibrate it internally and return it to service
D) Nothing: only the pilot may remove instruments
notes.choicesExplained: A: A&P technicians are not qualified for internal instrument maintenance. C: internal work needs specialised equipment and training. D: installation, removal and troubleshooting are field tasks for technicians.

notes.front: Why do electric instruments usually have a steel or iron alloy case?
notes.back: To contain the electromagnetic flux caused by current flowing inside.
notes.explanation: Other case materials include aluminium and magnesium alloys and plastic.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 10, “Instrument Housings & Handling”, p. 10-76
notes.evidence: Aluminum alloy, magnesium alloy, steel, iron, and plastic are all common materials for case construction. Electric instruments usually have a steel or iron alloy case to contain electromagnetic flux caused by current flow inside.

notes.front: You run a continuity check on an EGT harness with a hot heater probe placed over each thermocouple in turn. What result shows each thermocouple is working?
notes.back: C) The EGT indicator shows a temperature rise as each thermocouple is heated
notes.explanation: A probe heated to 500–700 °C over each thermocouple should give a rise on the EGT indicator, which finds inoperative thermocouples.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Continuity Check of Aircraft EGT Circuit”, p. 10-63
notes.evidence: The check is made by heating one heater probe to between 500 and 700 °C and placing the hot probe over each of the aircraft thermocouples, one at a time. The EGT indicator must show a temperature rise as each thermocouple is checked.
notes.choices:
A) The indicator stays steady
B) The analyser reads over 900 °C
C) The EGT indicator shows a temperature rise as each thermocouple is heated
D) The insulation meter reads zero ohms
notes.choicesExplained: A: a working thermocouple must produce a rise. B: probes must never exceed 900 °C. D: zero insulation resistance would suggest a short.

notes.front: During a continuity check of a harness with eight or more thermocouples, where is the reading taken, and why?
notes.back: On the analyser’s potentiometer; a rise is hard to see on the aircraft instrument because of the parallel circuit.
notes.explanation: The check cable and an adapter connect the analyser.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Continuity Check of Aircraft EGT Circuit”, p. 10-63
notes.evidence: When large numbers (eight or more) of thermocouples are used in the harness, it is difficult to see a rise on the aircraft instrument because of the electrical characteristics of a parallel circuit. Therefore, the temperature indication of the aircraft thermocouples is read on the potentiometer of the analyzer

notes.front: At what temperature is an EGT functional check usually made?
notes.back: The engine’s maximum operating temperature, found in the technical instructions.
notes.explanation: The analyser has a specific accuracy at that test temperature.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Functional Check of Aircraft EGT Circuit”, p. 10-63
notes.evidence: During the EGT system functional test and the thermocouple harness checks, the analyzer has a specific degree of accuracy at the test temperature, which is usually the maximum operating temperature of the turbine engine.

notes.front: What temperature must jetcal heater probes never exceed?
notes.explanation: Exceeding it damages the analyser and the heater probe assemblies.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Continuity Check of Aircraft EGT Circuit”, p. 10-63
notes.evidence: Never allow the heater probes to go over 900 °C (1,652 °F). Exceeding these temperatures results in damage to the jetcal analyzer and heater probe assemblies.

notes.front: Why is EGT thermocouple harness resistance held to very close tolerances?
notes.back: A change in resistance changes the current in the circuit and gives erroneous temperature readings.
notes.explanation: The analyser’s resistance and insulation circuits isolate such errors.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Resistance & Insulation Check”, p. 10-64
notes.evidence: The resistance of the thermocouple harness is held to very close tolerances, since a change in resistance changes the amount of current flow in the circuit. A change of resistance gives erroneous temperature readings.

notes.front: An EGT circuit has developed high resistance. How will the indicator read, and why does the handbook call it dangerous?
notes.back: B) It reads low while the engine may be running with excess temperature
notes.explanation: High circuit resistance gives a low indication, so the engine can be over temperature while the gauge looks normal.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Resistance of Circuit Out of Tolerance”, p. 10-65
notes.evidence: The engine thermocouple circuit resistance is a very important adjustment since a high-resistance condition gives a low indication on the aircraft EGT indicator. This condition is dangerous, because the engine is operating with excess temperature, but the high resistance makes the indicator read low.
notes.choices:
A) It reads high, so the crew reduces power unnecessarily
B) It reads low while the engine may be running with excess temperature
C) It fluctuates, which is harmless
D) It reads zero, which is obvious to the crew
notes.choicesExplained: A: high resistance makes the indicator read low. C: the handbook calls the low reading dangerous. D: it reads low, not zero, which hides the problem.

notes.front: What are two of the troubles an EGT analyser can isolate?
notes.back: Any two of: inoperative thermocouples, thermocouples out of calibration, indicator error, circuit resistance out of tolerance, shorts.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists six, including shorts to ground and shorts between leads.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Troubleshooting EGT System”, p. 10-64
notes.evidence: 1. One or more inoperative thermocouples in engine parallel harness. 2. Engine thermocouples out of calibration. 3. EGT indicator error. 4. Resistance of circuit out of tolerance. 5. Shorts to ground. 6. Shorts between leads.

notes.front: Individual thermocouples from a turbine harness read outside tolerance on a bench check with one heater probe. What does the handbook say causes such drift?
notes.back: C) Long exposure to oxidising atmospheres such as those in turbine engines
notes.explanation: Thermocouples exposed for a period to oxidising atmospheres drift appreciably from their original calibration.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Troubleshooting EGT System”, p. 10-64
notes.evidence: When thermocouples are subjected for a period of time to oxidizing atmospheres, such as encountered in turbine engines, they drift appreciably from their original calibration. On engine parallel harnesses, when individual thermocouples can be removed, these thermocouples can be bench-checked, using one heater probe.
notes.choices:
A) Using chromel and alumel
B) Coiling excess lead length
C) Long exposure to oxidising atmospheres such as those in turbine engines
D) Temperature compensation in the indicator
notes.choicesExplained: A: these are the normal turbine EGT metals. B: coiling is the approved way to handle long leads. D: compensation does not change the thermocouple itself.

notes.front: The analyser’s rpm check circuit reads engine speed during run-up with an accuracy of {{c1::±0.1 percent}}.
notes.back: ±0.1 percent.
notes.explanation: It reads engine speed during the run-up itself.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Troubleshooting Aircraft Tachometer System”, p. 10-65
notes.evidence: The rpm check circuit in the analyzer is used to read engine speed during engine run-up with an accuracy of ±0.1 percent.

notes.front: During run-up with the analyser in parallel, the aircraft tachometer and the rpm check circuit differ by more than the prescribed tolerance. What next?
notes.back: D) Stop the engine and locate and correct the trouble
notes.explanation: If the readings differ by more than the tolerance in the technical instructions, the engine must be stopped and the trouble located and corrected.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Troubleshooting Aircraft Tachometer System”, p. 10-65
notes.evidence: Both systems can be read simultaneously. If the difference between the readings of the aircraft tachometer indicator and the analyzer rpm check circuit exceeds the tolerance prescribed in applicable technical instructions, the engine must be stopped, and the trouble
notes.choices:
A) Continue the run and note it in the log
B) Accept the aircraft tachometer’s reading
C) Adjust the aircraft tachometer while running
D) Stop the engine and locate and correct the trouble
notes.choicesExplained: A: the handbook says the engine must be stopped. B: the analyser is the more accurate reference. C: the engine is stopped first, then the trouble is found.

notes.front: Which two engine instrument risks does the Airman Certification Standards ask applicants to manage?
notes.back: Maintenance damage to the instrument or indicating system, and engine instrument calibration or instrument error.
notes.explanation: They are the two risk management elements of its engine instrument systems task.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant Airman Certification Standards (FAA-S-ACS-1), “III. Powerplant, D. Engine Instrument Systems”, p. 47
notes.evidence: AM.III.D.R1 Maintenance damage to the instrument or indicating system. AM.III.D.R2 Engine instrument calibration or instrument error.
